words.meaning: to argue with a seller about the price of something
words.example: We haggled with the street seller for ten minutes and got the bag much cheaper.

words.meaning: to spend a lot of money on something nice you don't really need
words.example: On her birthday, she decided to splurge on a designer dress.
He is frugal and cooks at home instead of eating out.

words.meaning: careful and wise with money; not wasteful
words.example: My thrifty grandmother compares prices before she buys anything.

words.meaning: a sale to sell old stock at very low prices
words.example: The electronics store is holding a big clearance sale this weekend.

words.meaning: a written bill that shows what you must pay
words.example: The supplier sent an invoice for the new office chairs.

words.meaning: an extra charge added to the normal price
words.example: The airline added a fuel surcharge to every ticket.

words.meaning: a shop that sells famous brands at lower prices
words.example: We bought cheap shoes at the outlet mall outside the city.

words.meaning: the sale of goods directly to customers in shops
words.example: The retail price of the jacket is two hundred dollars.

words.meaning: the person who takes your money at a shop
words.example: The friendly cashier packed our groceries into paper bags.

grammar.title: 3B: Articles - a / an, the, no article
grammar.explanation:
Use **a** or **an** with singular countable nouns when you say what something is or what somebody does. She is **a** cashier in a big store.

Use **a/an** for the first mention of a thing or person. I found **a** clearance sale; **the** sale ends on Sunday.

Use **a/an** in exclamations with **What...!**. What **a** big surcharge on that invoice!

Use **a/an** in expressions of frequency. We visit the outlet **twice a month**.

Use **the** when you have already mentioned something, or when the meaning is clear. I saw **a** cashier, and **the** cashier helped me.

Use **the** for the only one of something, like **the** moon, and with superlatives. This is **the** cheapest outlet in town.

Use **the** with places in town, like **the** cinema or **the** theatre. We are meeting at **the** cinema near the outlet.

Use **no article** with plurals and uncountables when you speak in general. **Frugal** people check invoices; **thrifty** shoppers compare prices.

Use **no article** with **home**, **work**, **school** after **at**, **to**, **from**, and with meals, days, and months. She is at **work** now; we shop on **Fridays**.

Use **no article** before **next** or **last** plus a time word. See you **next** week at the outlet.

Articles work the same for every kind of shopper: people who **haggle** at markets, and people who **splurge** on **retail** brands.
examples: She is *a cashier* at the new outlet mall. (a/an: saying what somebody does)
I found *a clearance sale* near my office. (a/an: first mention)
What *a big surcharge* they added to the bill! (a/an: What...! exclamation)
We visit the outlet *twice a month*. (a/an: expressions of frequency)
I saw *an invoice* on the table. *The invoice* was for two hundred dollars. (the: already mentioned)
Please pay *the surcharge* before Friday. (the: clear reference)
This is *the cheapest* outlet in the city. (the: superlative)
We are meeting at *the cinema* after shopping. (the: places in town)
*Thrifty* shoppers always compare *retail* prices first. (no article: general plural)
He is *frugal* and he stays at *work* until six. (no article: at work)
*Haggle* on Mondays, *splurge* on Saturdays. (no article: days, in general)
See you *next week* at the outlet. (no article: next + week)
